case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a free, advertising-supported sports website that provides online video clips is a “video tape service provider” and/or whether its users are “consumers” under the Video Privacy Protection Act such that transmission of viewing data to third parties can trigger VPPA liability.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 2710 (the Video Privacy Protection Act of 1988), particularly the definitions and liability provisions in § 2710(a) and the disclosure prohibition in § 2710(b)(1).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Salazar argues the Sixth Circuit adopted an overly narrow, textually misguided interpretation of the VPPA that improperly limits the statute to businesses resembling 1980s video-rental models; he contends that modern websites offering video content (even free) can qualify as covered video service providers and that users can be “consumers,” so disclosure of their video-viewing information can be actionable under the VPPA. He further argues the case is an ideal vehicle to resolve an acknowledged circuit split because it comes to the Court on a final judgment without the procedural complications present in the related NBA petition.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Paramount/247Sports argues certiorari should be denied because the VPPA was aimed at video rental/sales records and does not fit a free sports news site that provides articles, photos, and video clips; it emphasizes that 247Sports does not rent, sell, or offer subscriptions to videotapes and does not stream movies or shows, so the statutory terms do not cover its business. It also argues the petition is a poor vehicle because (even if the Court addressed the ‘consumer’ issue) Salazar’s complaint would fail on other independent grounds, and the Court should let the issues continue to percolate among circuits rather than take this case.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to warn against freezing the VPPA in 1988, and “delivery” plus “similar audiovisual materials” can reach modern distribution in some settings. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, those terms operate inside a threshold definition—an entity must be “engaged in the business” of renting, selling, or delivering materials akin to video cassettes—and Yates’s contextual approach makes it hard to treat an ad-supported sports news site with incidental clips as that kind of provider without effectively erasing the limiter. Justice Jackson’s concern about courts smuggling a paid-subscription requirement into “consumer” is important, but it is downstream: resolving this case on the antecedent “video tape service provider” question avoids any extra-textual subscription test while keeping the statute coherent and bounded. The circuit cases Justice Sotomayor points to (e.g., Eichenberger and Perry) do not unsettle that narrow path because they largely assume provider status and address PII/standing, not the definitional fit of a publisher-with-clips to § 2710(a)(4).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “technology-neutral” argument presses a real policy concern, but under an original public-meaning and contextual reading, § 2710(a)(4) does not regulate every entity that transmits video; it reaches those “engaged in the business” of renting, selling, or delivering materials akin to “prerecorded video cassette tapes.” As Justice Gorsuch explains using Yates-style associated-words reasoning, “similar audiovisual materials” is bounded by the videocassette-rental/sales paradigm rather than incidental clips on an ad-supported news site, and purpose cannot dissolve that limiting context. Justice Jackson’s worry about courts grafting a subscription/payment requirement is largely downstream: as Justice Kagan notes, “consumer” status is tethered to obtaining goods or services from a qualifying “video tape service provider,” so the definitional threshold does the work here. The modern-application cases Justice Sotomayor cites (e.g., Eichenberger, Perry) do not alter the analysis because they largely assume provider-status or address injury/PII rather than the antecedent statutory definition at issue.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s concern that the Sixth Circuit effectively smuggles in a paid-subscription or account-like requirement for “subscriber” is the most serious pushback, but it remains downstream of the threshold definition: the plaintiff must first show the defendant is a “video tape service provider” “engaged in the business” of renting, selling, or delivering videocassette-like materials. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize (invoking Yates-style contextual canons), reading “delivery” and “similar audio visual materials” in isolation would erase that business-limiting language and effectively convert the VPPA into a general internet-tracking statute whenever a site hosts incidental clips. Justice Sotomayor’s technology-neutral point has force as a policy matter, but under a textualist approach the statute’s enumerated commercial paradigms (“renter, purchaser, or subscriber”) and the videocassette-centered framing constrain “similar” to analogous video-distribution enterprises, not ad-supported news publishing with embedded video. The cited modern VPPA cases (e.g., Eichenberger, Perry) largely assume provider status or turn on injury/PII, so they do not undermine resolving the antecedent definitional mismatch here and avoiding sweeping, impractical liability absent clearer congressional direction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest counter is Justice Kagan’s and the Chief Justice’s Yates-based concern that reading “delivery” and “similar audiovisual materials” broadly will erase the “engaged in the business” limiter and effectively turn the VPPA into a general internet-tracking statute. But that workability fear cannot justify narrowing Congress’s chosen, technology-neutral terms where the statute itself already supplies limiting principles: the defendant must be “engaged in the business” of delivering audiovisual materials (not merely hosting a stray clip), and liability attaches only for disclosure of “personally identifiable information” tied to a consumer’s viewing history—so routine, non-identifying analytics still fall out. Justice Gorsuch’s Fischer point about not divorcing general words from context cuts the other way here: the context is a privacy statute targeting disclosure of viewing records, and online video delivery is the modern analog of the distribution Congress sought to regulate, not an atextual expansion. The institutional “leave it to Congress” argument (Roberts/Thomas/Alito) is serious, but in my methodological view we do more institutional harm by creating a privacy gap Congress wrote against simply because the dominant business model evolved from paid rentals to ad-supported delivery.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s technology-neutral point is serious, but on my pragmatic textualist view it cannot override § 2710(a)(4)’s threshold limiter: the statute reaches only entities “engaged in the business” of renting, selling, or delivering “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” and under the contextual approach Justice Gorsuch invokes (Yates/Fischer), “similar” takes its meaning from the videocassette-distribution paradigm rather than incidental clips on an ad-supported news site. Justice Jackson is right to resist importing a paid-subscription or account requirement into “consumer,” but that dispute is downstream because “consumer” status exists only by obtaining goods or services from a qualifying “video tape service provider,” so provider-status does the necessary screening. The circuit cases Justice Sotomayor cites (Eichenberger, Perry) do not materially undermine this because they largely assume provider status and address PII/injury questions rather than the antecedent definitional fit here. Reading “delivery” to cover any transmission of any video would, as the Chief Justice stresses, effectively erase the business-focused limiter and make the VPPA operate like a general internet-tracking statute without clearer congressional instruction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that “delivery” and “similar audio visual materials” are technology-neutral and can reach online video—does not answer the statute’s threshold limiter: only entities “engaged in the business” of renting, selling, or delivering items like “prerecorded video cassette tapes” qualify, and under Yates’s associated-words reasoning that context narrows “similar” to a video-distribution enterprise rather than a general sports-news site with ancillary clips. Justice Jackson is right to caution against grafting a paid-subscription requirement onto “consumer,” but that debate is downstream because § 2710(a)(1) makes “consumer” derivative of obtaining goods or services from a “video tape service provider,” so provider-status must be satisfied first. The circuit decisions Sotomayor cites (e.g., Eichenberger, Perry) largely assume provider status and focus on injury/PII, so they do not undermine a narrow holding on the definitional “engaged in the business” question here. Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional concern about converting the VPPA into a general internet-tracking regime reinforces—not substitutes for—the textual point that such a major expansion requires clearer congressional authorization.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s concern that lower courts may be importing an extra-textual paid “subscription” requirement is a fair caution about the definition of “consumer,” but it remains downstream of the antecedent question whether the defendant is a “video tape service provider” at all. As the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize (invoking Yates/Fischer-style contextualism), the statute’s limiting phrase “engaged in the business” and the company kept by “prerecorded video cassette tapes” materially narrows “similar audio visual materials,” making an ad-supported sports news site with incidental clips a poor fit for the covered class. Justice Sotomayor’s technology-neutral appeal and reliance on cases like Eichenberger and Perry does not dislodge that threshold reading because those decisions largely assume provider status and focus elsewhere (injury/PII), rather than answering the definitional tether Congress wrote in 1988. Given the institutional and workability concerns identified by Chief Justice Roberts—avoiding a judicial transformation of the VPPA into a broad internet-tracking regime absent clearer congressional direction—I remain with Respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s technology-neutral argument has force at the level of isolated words like “delivery” and “similar audiovisual materials,” but Yates’s contextual method—emphasized by Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch—requires reading those terms in company with “rental” and “sale” of “prerecorded video cassette tapes,” which narrows the provider category to a video-distribution enterprise rather than a general news site with ancillary clips. Justice Jackson’s concern about importing a paid-subscription or account-like requirement is answered by the statute’s structure: “consumer” status depends on obtaining goods or services “from a video tape service provider,” so broadening “subscriber” cannot extend liability beyond entities that satisfy § 2710(a)(4) in the first place. The circuit decisions Sotomayor invokes (e.g., Eichenberger, Perry) do not materially shift the analysis because they largely assume provider status or address injury/PII, leaving the antecedent definitional question open here. Absent clearer congressional authorization, reading “delivery” to cover any web transmission would effectively erase the “engaged in the business” limiter and transform the VPPA into a general internet-tracking statute, which the text does not support.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take seriously Justice Kagan’s and the Chief Justice’s strongest point: “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery” must do real limiting work, and we should not convert the VPPA into a general internet-tracking statute by reading “delivery” in isolation. But the Sixth Circuit’s approach, as described by Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch, risks doing its own atextual narrowing by treating an ad-supported model and the absence of a paid account relationship as dispositive of being “in the business” and of “subscriber” status, despite Congress’s technology-neutral phrasing and the statute’s focus on disclosure of identified viewing records. Yates/Fischer-style contextual canons can narrow “similar audiovisual materials” to genuine video-delivery enterprises without freezing the statute to videocassette-era transaction forms, and the privacy harm Congress targeted can occur through modern “delivery” just as readily as through rental or sale. The precedents colleagues cite (e.g., Eichenberger and Perry) may not resolve provider-status, but they underscore that courts have applied VPPA to modern video delivery without importing a payment requirement, which reinforces my concern about creating an arbitrary privacy gap for users whose viewing histories are monetized without meaningful choice.

John Roberts.reasoning: The VPPA’s operative prohibition applies to a “video tape service provider” disclosing “personally identifiable information” about a “consumer,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a), (b)(1), and those defined terms are textually anchored to entities engaged in renting, selling, or delivering “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.” On this record, a free, advertising-supported sports website offering incidental clips is a poor fit for that statutory core, and expanding coverage to such websites risks converting a targeted privacy statute into a broad internet-tracking regime better left to Congress—an institutional-legitimacy concern favoring restraint. Even circuits recognizing VPPA standing (e.g., Eichenberger v. ESPN) do not resolve the antecedent definitional question presented here, and the acknowledged disagreement among lower courts counsels allowing further percolation rather than issuing an expansive construction on an imperfect vehicle. A narrow, precedent-respecting approach therefore favors affirming the Sixth Circuit’s limitation of VPPA liability to businesses more closely resembling the statute’s contemplated video-delivery services.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying the VPPA’s text as it was publicly understood in 1988, a free, advertising-supported sports news website offering incidental video clips is not “engaged in the business . . . of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), because its business is news and advertising rather than the delivery of audiovisual materials as a commercial service. On that original public meaning, a site visitor likewise is not a “consumer” absent a rental, purchase, or subscription relationship tied to such delivery, § 2710(a)(1), and we should not expand those terms beyond their historical and textual limits to reach modern web-tracking practices. The Court has cautioned against stretching criminal/civil-liability statutes to novel settings untethered from their ordinary meaning and context, see Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015), and the Sixth Circuit’s narrower reading better respects Congress’s chosen words and the limits of federal power. Whatever privacy concerns exist today are for Congress to address by updating the statute, not for courts to rewrite it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The VPPA’s text targets entities “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and its paired definition of “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber,” § 2710(a)(1), is most naturally read to cover transactional relationships akin to the enumerated forms of distribution. Applying the limiting canons recognized in Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015), “similar audio visual materials” should be construed in light of “prerecorded video cassette tapes,” not expanded to encompass every free, ad-supported website that hosts short clips, which would create sweeping and impractical liability untethered to Congress’s 1988 design. On this record, 247Sports is not plausibly “in the business” of renting, selling, or delivering VPPA-covered materials in the statutory sense, and the statute should not be stretched to regulate modern advertising pixels absent clearer congressional direction. The practical consequences of extending a criminally enforceable privacy statute to broad swaths of the Internet confirm the wisdom of adhering to the statute’s narrow terms rather than adopting an atextual, technology-driven expansion.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The VPPA’s text is technology-neutral: it covers any person “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and prohibits disclosure of “personally identifiable information” identifying what videos a “consumer” requested or obtained, § 2710(b)(1), (a)(1), (a)(3). Limiting “delivery” and “similar audio visual materials” to 1980s rental-store models would undercut Congress’s core privacy aim in § 2710(b)(1) and leave modern users—often with the least power to bargain over data practices—without the statute’s protections. The better reading, consistent with the privacy-harm analysis embraced by multiple circuits, is that disclosures of viewing data tied to an identifier can be actionable because they implicate traditional invasion-of-privacy interests, as recognized in Eichenberger v. ESPN, Inc., 876 F.3d 979, 982–84 (9th Cir. 2017), and Perry v. Cable News Network, Inc., 854 F.3d 1336, 1340–41 (11th Cir. 2017), rather than being dismissed as a mismatch with contemporary distribution methods. Given the acknowledged circuit disagreement over the statute’s definitional reach in digital contexts and the real-world consequences of pervasive tracking, I would vote to interpret the VPPA to encompass online video-delivery services and their users where the statutory elements are plausibly alleged.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The VPPA’s definitions must be read in their full statutory context, not by giving isolated words their maximum breadth: a “video tape service provider” is one “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), which most naturally targets entities whose business is providing video as such, not a free, ad-supported sports news site where video clips are incidental to a broader editorial product. As in Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015), the Court should resist stretching an older, technology-inflected statute beyond the limits suggested by text, structure, and purpose; “similar audio visual materials” cannot be read to convert every website with some video into a covered “video tape service provider” without collapsing the statute’s business-limiting language. Even if “consumer” includes some “subscribers” under § 2710(a)(1), that definition is tethered to obtaining “goods or services from a video tape service provider,” so the threshold provider-status question is dispositive here. A cramped but workable reading preserves statutory coherence and avoids turning VPPA into a general internet-tracking tort absent clearer congressional instruction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The VPPA’s definitions must be read in statutory context, not by giving isolated words their broadest imaginable meaning. Section 2710(a)(4) ties a “video tape service provider” to a business engaged in “rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” and under noscitur a sociis/associated-words principles applied in Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015), the general phrase “similar audio visual materials” is best understood as referring to a video-rental/sales type enterprise rather than an advertising-supported sports news site incidentally offering short clips. Reading the statute to cover any website that ‘delivers’ any video would risk untethering the VPPA from the text Congress enacted and creating sweeping civil liability without a clear statement, a concern this Court has repeatedly addressed by enforcing contextual limits in cases like Yates and Fischer v. United States, 603 U.S. 480 (2024). On that reading, 247Sports is not a covered “video tape service provider,” and the VPPA’s disclosure prohibition in § 2710(b)(1) is not triggered.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Reading the VPPA in historical and textual context, its key definitions—“video tape service provider” and “consumer” in 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)—are naturally tied to a business model involving the rental, sale, or delivery of “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” not a free, advertising-supported sports news site offering incidental clips. Under Yates v. United States and Fischer v. United States, we avoid an acontextual overbreadth that would give general terms an expansive meaning inconsistent with their associated, historically specific words; here, that counsel cuts against transforming a broad swath of ad-supported websites into VPPA-covered providers. Given judicial restraint and practical workability concerns, expanding VPPA liability to routine online analytics and third-party transmissions without clearer congressional direction risks sweeping consequences beyond the statute’s evident 1988 design. I would therefore vote to affirm the narrower construction that excludes respondent’s website (and thus deny liability on these facts).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The VPPA’s text, read in context, defines a “video tape service provider” as one “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and the associated canons counsel against stretching “delivery” to sweep in a free, advertising-supported sports site whose principal business is news content with incidental clips. As in Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015), we should interpret general terms in light of their statutory neighbors (noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis) and the overall scheme, which targets disclosures of records tied to obtaining video materials or services in a way akin to rental/sale/subscription models. That contextual reading also promotes methodological consistency and avoids converting the VPPA into a broad internet-tracking statute untethered from the “similar audiovisual materials” limitation in § 2710(a)(4), leaving any modernization to Congress. Given these textual constraints, I would not extend VPPA coverage here on the theory that any website transmitting video clips “delivers” covered materials to “consumers” under § 2710(a)(1).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I would vote for Petitioner because the Sixth Circuit’s narrowing construction appears to add a subscription-like requirement to the VPPA’s definition of “consumer” that is not found in the text, which covers any “renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1). Given the statute’s privacy-protective purpose and the practical realities of modern video delivery, an ad-supported website that provides video clips can plausibly be a “video tape service provider” under § 2710(a)(4), and users who obtain access (even without payment) can qualify as “subscribers” of the site’s video “services.” The acknowledged circuit conflict—reflected in decisions like Eichenberger v. ESPN and Perry v. CNN—warrants resolution, and treating disclosure of viewing data as a concrete privacy injury aligns with those courts’ Article III analysis and with the VPPA’s substantive right against disclosure in § 2710(b)(1). A pragmatic, fairness-oriented approach favors allowing the claim to proceed where the alleged conduct fits the statutory prohibition and implicates the precise privacy harm Congress targeted.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a free sports-news website that publishes online video clips qualifies as a “video tape service provider” under the Video Privacy Protection Act such that it can be liable for disclosing users’ viewing information, and (secondarily) whether the alleged statutory violation alone confers Article III standing.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 2710 (Video Privacy Protection Act, including definitions such as § 2710(a)(4) and § 2710(a)(3), and the disclosure prohibition in § 2710(b)(1)); U.S. Const. art. III standing doctrine (as applied in Spokeo and TransUnion).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Salazar argues the Sixth Circuit adopted an unduly narrow, atextual reading of the VPPA (particularly the scope of who is covered as a video service provider/consumer in the modern streaming-and-online-video context). He contends the Act should apply to websites offering video content even if the videos are free, and that the Court should grant certiorari because there is a circuit split and this case is a clean vehicle with a final judgment and no ongoing proceedings below—unlike the related NBA petition—so the Court can resolve the interpretive conflict now.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Paramount Global/247Sports argues certiorari should be denied and, on the merits, that the VPPA is aimed at businesses akin to video rental/sales services and does not cover a free sports news website offering articles, photos, and short video clips. It also contends Salazar’s suit fails on multiple independent grounds (making the case a poor vehicle), and emphasizes that in circuits with controlling precedent on key VPPA issues the complaint would fail as a matter of law. Respondent further suggests continued percolation is preferable given multiple developing circuit splits (including tests for “personally identifiable information”).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—rooted in TransUnion—that “disclosure of private information” can be a concrete injury is not lost on me, but her analogy falters on the nature and scope of the alleged disclosure here: a transmission to a single analytics/advertising intermediary without pleaded dissemination or downstream consequences remains closer to a bare statutory-violation theory than to the historically grounded privacy torts TransUnion requires us to use as a guide. On the merits, I find Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s textual point especially persuasive: the VPPA’s tightly linked definitions (“video tape service provider” and “consumer” as “renter, purchaser, or subscriber”) tether “delivery” to a video-service business relationship, and reading it to cover any ad-supported site with embedded clips risks untethered, effectively boundless coverage. Under a minimalist approach that protects institutional legitimacy, the narrowest sound path is to resolve this case on Article III standing (and, in the alternative, the provider-definition threshold), leaving any broader internet-privacy modernization to Congress rather than stretching a 1988 statute beyond its textual limits.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s technology-neutral reading of “delivery” is the strongest case for petitioner, and I accept that TransUnion recognizes some disclosure-based harms as concrete. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the original public meaning is fixed by the VPPA’s linked definitions: a “video tape service provider” must be “engaged in the business” of “rental, sale, or delivery” of “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” and the only protected “consumer” is a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber,” which textually presupposes a service-relationship model rather than incidental, ad-supported clips on a general website. TransUnion cannot be used to expand statutory coverage; if respondent is not within the 1988 definition, there is no cause of action regardless of the concreteness of the alleged injury. I would affirm on the statutory-coverage ground and thus need not resolve the most difficult standing questions in this posture.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s technology-neutral point about “delivery” and “similar audiovisual materials” has force as a matter of policy, but it cannot overcome the statute’s tightly linked definitional structure: as Justice Barrett emphasizes, noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis and the paired “consumer” definition (“renter, purchaser, or subscriber”) tether the VPPA to a transactional, video-service business model rather than a general, ad-supported website with embedded clips. Justice Jackson’s standing argument relying on TransUnion is also incomplete here because TransUnion demands a close relationship to historically recognized harms; disclosure to a single analytics/advertising intermediary, without allegations resembling public disclosure or concrete downstream misuse, looks closer to a bare statutory-violation theory than to common-law publicity-type torts. Even if some disclosures can be concrete, that does not license an atextual expansion of “video tape service provider” to cover routine internet data flows—an update Congress can make expressly. I therefore remain with respondent on statutory coverage, with standing as an additional obstacle in this posture.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and the Chief Justice’s contextual point—that “consumer” as “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” suggests a service-relationship and cabins “engaged in the business”—is the most serious textual constraint, but it does not compel excluding ad-supported, registration-based streaming where users effectively “subscribe” in the ordinary sense and the site regularly delivers prerecorded clips as a product feature. Justice Barrett’s noscitur/ejusdem generis argument properly guards against boundless coverage, yet it cannot be used to erase Congress’s deliberately broader term “delivery” in a three-part list (rental/sale/delivery) that is naturally capable of capturing non-tape distribution of prerecorded audiovisual works. On standing, Justice Roberts and Justice Alito read TransUnion too narrowly: TransUnion explicitly treats unauthorized disclosure of private information as a concrete injury, and an alleged transmission of identified viewing history to a third-party analytics/advertising intermediary is the invasion itself, not a mere procedural defect requiring further downstream misuse. Under a pragmatic reading attentive to real-world privacy harms and statutory evolution, respondent’s approach risks nullifying the VPPA whenever video moves platforms, contrary to the Act’s core protection.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the best case that “delivery” and “similar audiovisual materials” can be read technology-neutrally and that VPPA’s privacy purpose should not evaporate with streaming, but the statute’s structure still matters: “engaged in the business” is linked to “rental, sale, or delivery” and the adjacent definition of “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” (as Justice Barrett emphasizes) strongly signals a video-service relationship, not incidental clips on a general news site. On standing, TransUnion’s recognition of disclosure-based harms helps petitioner in the abstract, yet here the pleaded transmission to a single analytics/advertising intermediary—without allegations of broader dissemination or concrete downstream effects—tracks Chief Justice Roberts’s concern that we would be treating a routine data flow as a per se concrete injury, collapsing TransUnion’s “close relationship” requirement. Under a pragmatic textualist approach, affirming on the provider-definition threshold yields a workable, coherent reading that avoids converting the VPPA into a general internet-privacy code better left to Congress. I therefore remain with respondent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that “delivery” and “similar audiovisual materials” should be read technology-neutrally and that TransUnion treats disclosure of private information as concrete harm—has force at a high level, but it does not answer the statute’s threshold, entity-definitional limits. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, the VPPA’s coverage turns on whether the defendant is “engaged in the business” of “rental, sale, or delivery” of “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar” materials, and the paired “consumer” definition (“renter, purchaser, or subscriber”) reinforces that Congress had a video-service, tape-like distribution relationship in view, not a general news site with incidental clips. Even if TransUnion can support standing where there is a close analogue to historically recognized disclosure harms, Article III cannot supply a cause of action where the statute—read in its full textual and structural context—does not reach the defendant in the first place. I therefore would affirm on statutory coverage, with standing as an additional obstacle in this case’s posture, and I do not think Justice Jackson’s administrability response cures the textual mismatch.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that “delivery” and “similar audiovisual materials” are broad enough to cover streaming and that TransUnion recognizes disclosure harms—deserves full credit, but it still runs into the statute’s paired, transactional architecture: “video tape service provider” is defined by being “engaged in the business” of rental/sale/delivery, and “consumer” is limited to a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber,” which (as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize) tethers coverage to a video-service relationship rather than incidental clips on a free general website. On standing, even taking Justice Jackson’s view that “actual transmission” to a third party can be an injury, TransUnion’s requirement of a harm closely related to a traditionally recognized privacy tort is not satisfied by allegations of routine backend sharing with a single analytics/advertising intermediary absent pleaded publicity, misuse, or other real-world consequences; otherwise we effectively adopt a statutory-violation-is-enough rule the Court rejected. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional concern that expanding a 1988 statute into a general internet-privacy regime without clear congressional direction is not our role, and it creates serious administrability problems untethered from the enacted text. I therefore remain for respondent, with the statutory-coverage limit as the cleanest ground and standing as an additional barrier in this posture.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that “delivery” and “similar audiovisual materials” can be read in a technology-neutral way to reach streaming, and that TransUnion recognizes disclosure of private information as potentially concrete. But as Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, the statute’s tightly linked definitions—provider engaged in the business of rental/sale/delivery of cassette-like materials and “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber”—signal a transactional video-service relationship; under noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis, that structure prevents the VPPA from expanding to incidental clips on a general news site. On standing, TransUnion’s disclosure rationale still requires a close relationship to historically recognized harms, and here the alleged transmission to a single analytics/advertising intermediary without pleaded publicity or downstream misuse looks closer to the “bare statutory violation” side of the line Justice Kagan identifies. Nothing in Justice Jackson’s administrability response overcomes the textual mismatch between “consumer” and a casual website visitor, so I remain for respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make the strongest textual/administrability point: tethering “delivery” to “rental” and “sale,” plus the “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” consumer definition, risks turning VPPA into a boundless internet-privacy statute if we read it to cover any site with video. But I think that concern is addressed by the statute’s own narrowing terms—“engaged in the business” and “consumer”—which allow courts to distinguish websites that regularly provide video content to users from those where video is truly incidental, without carving streaming out of “delivery” categorically. On standing, Justice Alito’s TransUnion argument matters, yet TransUnion also recognizes disclosure of private information as a concrete injury; an alleged actual transmission of identified viewing data to a third party is the harm itself, closely analogous to traditional disclosure-based privacy torts even if not “publicity” to the world. Under my pragmatic, consequences-attentive approach, respondents’ narrowing constructions would significantly undercut the VPPA’s core privacy protection in modern distribution settings absent clearer statutory language compelling that limitation.

John Roberts.reasoning: The VPPA’s definition of a “video tape service provider” as one “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), is best read—consistent with the statute’s targeted purpose and text—to cover entities whose business is providing video content as a service, not a general free sports-news site that incidentally posts short clips. Even if the complaint pleads a technical statutory violation, Article III requires a concrete injury; under TransUnion, a plaintiff cannot rely on a bare statutory violation divorced from a harm closely related to a traditionally recognized privacy injury, and the alleged disclosure here is not shown to have caused such concrete harm. A narrow disposition on standing avoids an expansive interpretation of an older statute in a fast-changing technological setting and preserves institutional legitimacy while leaving room for Congress to update the law if warranted. Because multiple independent defects are asserted, deciding on standing grounds also fits the Court’s preference for minimal, case-specific resolution.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The VPPA defines a “video tape service provider” as one engaged in the business of the “rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and the ordinary public meaning in 1988 ties “delivery” to furnishing tape-like prerecorded works in a commercial distribution model, not the incidental posting of free online news clips on a general-interest website. Read textually and in context with the parallel definition of “consumer” (“renter, purchaser, or subscriber” of goods or services from such a provider), § 2710(a)(1), the statute targets businesses akin to video rental/sales/delivery services, not any publisher that happens to embed video. Even if a statutory violation were alleged, Article III requires a concrete injury beyond a bare statutory violation as emphasized in TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez and Spokeo; disclosure claims untethered to concrete harm do not automatically satisfy standing. Because petitioner’s reading would expand the statute beyond its text and original public meaning, I would affirm for respondent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Video Privacy Protection Act’s text targets an “entity engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), language that naturally connotes a business whose commercial enterprise is providing video content—not a general, free sports-news website that incidentally offers short clips. Reading “delivery … of … similar audiovisual materials” to sweep in any website with embedded video would expand the statute far beyond its video-store-era focus and create significant practical consequences by converting routine online analytics and advertising integrations into federal privacy torts. Independently, under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, a bare statutory violation does not itself establish Article III standing absent a concrete injury with a close relationship to traditionally recognized harms; allegations of automated transmission of viewing data, without plausibly alleged real-world harm, are insufficient. Given the multiple independent grounds respondent identifies, the narrower construction avoids turning VPPA into a broad, atextual internet-privacy regime better left to Congress.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The VPPA’s text is technology-neutral: a “video tape service provider” includes any person “engaged in the business… of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and online video clips are at least “similar audiovisual materials” delivered to consumers, even if access is free, where the website’s business includes delivering video content. Reading the statute to exclude modern, ad-supported online video platforms would undercut Congress’s evident remedial purpose—preventing disclosure of individuals’ viewing choices—and would especially harm vulnerable users for whom viewing history can reveal sensitive beliefs and associations, § 2710(b)(1). On standing, an alleged disclosure of identified viewing information to a third party plausibly constitutes a concrete injury at the pleading stage because it closely resembles traditional privacy harms, which TransUnion recognizes as concrete (including “disclosure of private information”), 594 U.S. 413, 141 S. Ct. 2190, 2204 (2021). Therefore, I would favor granting relief on the merits consistent with the statute’s broad privacy-protective design and TransUnion’s guidance on intangible privacy injuries.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The VPPA’s definition of “video tape service provider” covers a person “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and read in statutory context (including “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber,” § 2710(a)(1)) it is best understood to target entities whose business is providing video content as a service, not a general-interest, free sports-news site that incidentally embeds short clips. Under a pragmatic, coherent reading of “similar audiovisual materials,” the term should be tethered to the Act’s rental/sale/delivery business model and not stretched to any website that hosts videos, which would make the definition essentially limitless and administratively unworkable (cf. Yates v. United States; Fischer v. United States, emphasizing contextual and coherent statutory interpretation). Even if the complaint pleads disclosure to a third party, TransUnion requires a concrete injury closely related to a traditionally recognized harm, and disclosure to a single platform for analytics/advertising—without plausible “publicity” or downstream consequences—pushes toward a “bare statutory violation” theory rather than the common-law analogue. Given those textual and standing concerns, I would affirm the judgment for respondent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The VPPA covers only a person “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and the ordinary meaning of “similar” cabins the statute to businesses dealing in video products analogous to prerecorded cassettes—not a free, ad-supported sports-news website whose principal business is publishing articles and incidentally hosting clips. Reading “delivery” to sweep in any website that streams video would disregard the statutory context (including the “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” limitation in § 2710(a)(1)) and effectively amend a 1988 statute to cover the modern Internet, contrary to a textualist approach. Even if the statute were violated, Article III requires a concrete injury; under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez and Spokeo, a bare statutory violation without a close historical analogue to a traditionally cognizable harm does not suffice. Because the complaint does not plausibly allege respondent is a covered “video tape service provider,” the judgment should be affirmed.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Reading the VPPA in light of its text and historical context, a free sports-news website that incidentally offers short video clips is not plausibly a “video tape service provider” engaged in the “rental, sale, or delivery” of “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials” within the meaning of 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and we should be reluctant to expand a 1988 statute beyond its evident core without clearer congressional direction. Even if petitioner alleges a statutory violation, Article III requires a concrete injury, and under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, a bare violation untethered to a traditionally recognized harm is insufficient; the most analogous concrete harm arises only when the plaintiff’s viewing information is actually disclosed to a third party in a way resembling invasion of privacy. Given the statute’s focus, the need for administrable limits, and the Court’s duty of judicial restraint, I would affirm the Sixth Circuit’s narrower construction rather than adopt an atextual, boundless rule that sweeps in general-content websites. Practical workability and institutional legitimacy counsel leaving any major modernization of the VPPA’s coverage to Congress, not the Court.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The VPPA’s text defines a covered “video tape service provider” as one “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and the associated “consumer” definition is keyed to “renter,” “purchaser,” and “subscriber,” § 2710(a)(1). Read in ordinary meaning and with the canon of noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis, “similar audio visual materials” is best understood as materials akin to prerecorded tapes offered in a rental/sale/delivery business, not incidental short clips embedded on a free sports-news site—consistent with the statute’s paired structure and the narrowing approach reflected in cases applying these canons in modern contexts (cf. Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015)). Even if a broader reading were plausible, Article III requires a concrete injury beyond a bare statutory violation, and under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021), an alleged unlawful disclosure without a pleaded real-world harm or close historical analogue would not suffice. Given these independent barriers, the complaint’s theory does not fit the statute’s original public meaning and also raises standing concerns under TransUnion and Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The VPPA’s text covers any “person, engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials” (18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4)), and in today’s market “delivery” of “similar audio visual materials” reasonably encompasses a website that regularly provides streaming video clips to users, even if the content is free, because the statute does not condition coverage on payment. Reading the Act to exclude modern online video services risks undermining Congress’s core privacy purpose—preventing disclosure of a person’s viewing history—based on outdated distribution technology, a consequence I am reluctant to adopt absent clear statutory language. On standing, an alleged wrongful disclosure of viewing information is not a “bare procedural violation” but an invasion of a privacy interest with a close common-law analogue (public disclosure of private facts), satisfying Article III under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021), when the complaint alleges actual transmission of viewing data to a third party. Because the Sixth Circuit’s narrow construction threatens to defeat the statute’s protections in the contemporary streaming context, I would vote for the Petitioner.
